Readings / Domestic remittances and accounts: what the evidence establishes
Reading

What does the published evidence establish about whether adults in Yemen who received domestic remittances received them into an account of their own?

Domestic remittances and accounts: what the evidence establishes

Report an error

In Yemen’s Global Findex 2021 wave, 31.9% of adults in surveyed areas received domestic remittances and 11.9% of adults in those areas had an account at a financial institution. For that wave, no weighted estimate of the channel usable here is published or held (the database’s printed zero for receipt into an account conflicts with the World Bank’s own documentation and is not used); the World Bank’s published variable documentation records that recipients were asked whether they received the money using a bank or mobile-money account, and that some answered yes. That money sent between people reaches recipients more through exchange companies and other money-transfer providers than into accounts of their own remains a hypothesis: the survey counts adults, not households, and its values here cover transfers within Yemen only. Other routes, such as cash carried by hand, and humanitarian cash fit the same numbers, and survey coverage, currency and the meaning of “remittance” limit what they show.

Evidence periodGlobal Findex 2021, Yemen fieldwork November 2022 – January 2023 · World Bank country profile for 2014 · CBY-Aden roster for 2026 · CBY-Aden domestic-transfer rule of June 2024 · remittance prices for 2023 and 2025 Q3 · CBY-Aden annual reports 2024 and 2025 · Cash Consortium of Yemen studies of aid recipients (survey data of January and June 2024)
Last reviewed11 October 2026

What not to conclude

A share of adults who received domestic remittances is not a share of households that depend on them; the bound that CauseWay calculates from the two published shares (at least 62.7% of recipients in surveyed areas without an account at a financial institution, itself a survey estimate) describes the group, not any individual recipient, does not establish the channel, and does not rule out an account type for which no Yemen value is published; a roster entry or a branch count is not a measure of remittance flows; and a price of sending money from abroad is not the cost a household pays to collect it.

01Weighted channel values are old, and providers are listed, not measured02A hypothesis, not a finding03Other explanations and limits04Price and scale are measured for money from abroad05Where the evidence stops06How to use the figures07What would change this reading?08Trace the evidence09Sources10Related measurement priorities11Related readings

A larger share of adults in Yemen’s surveyed areas received money from within the country than held an account, but the published values do not say how that money travelled. In the World Bank’s Global Findex 2021 wave for Yemen, fielded from November 2022 to January 2023, 17.7% of adults in surveyed areas sent domestic remittances, 31.9% received them and 37.8% did either; 11.9% of adults had an account at a financial institution. Each is a share of all adults, from its own question or, for “either”, from the two combined, so the figures give no exact count of the recipients who had an account. The two shares do bound it: by CauseWay’s calculation from them, at most 11.9% of adults can be both, so at least 62.7% of the adults in surveyed areas who received domestic remittances did not have an account at a financial institution. Both shares are survey estimates, so the bound is an estimate too, not an exact floor; it is a bound on the group, not a statement about any individual. It does not establish the channel: it bears only on whether recipients could have received the money into a financial-institution account of their own, does not show how they did receive it or how many used an exchange company, and does not rule out a mobile wallet or another account type for which the World Bank publishes no Yemen value. The World Bank also publishes the sending and receiving shares by sex, age, education, income and labour-force status, in the table on /people/; no interval is published here for a group value, and a difference between groups is not a cause.

The survey counts adults, not households, and the values here cover transfers within Yemen only.

Weighted channel values are old, and providers are listed, not measured

The only weighted channel values held here are historical. The World Bank’s weighted country profile for 2014 reports that 18.3% of adults received domestic remittances; among those recipients, 31.1% received them through a money transfer operator and 2.0% through a financial institution. These are shares of recipients, not of all adults; they do not show how much money moved through each channel, and they do not describe the situation today. For the 2021 wave, no weighted estimate of the channel for domestic remittances usable here is published or held. The World Bank’s published variable documentation for that wave records that recipients were asked whether they received the money using a bank or mobile-money account and that some answered yes; these are unweighted counts of answers, not an estimate for the population, and they are not used here. The World Bank’s database prints zero for receipt into an account, with no recipient or group value; the two statements cannot both describe the same quantity, so the printed value is not used either. The World Bank publishes no mobile-money-account figure for Yemen, and its figure for an account at a financial institution is the same as its account figure.

On the supply side, the official 2026 roster of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) lists 100 exchange companies, 231 individual exchange establishments and 111 remittance agents. These are entries counted by the roster’s own classes, not a count of unique providers or of providers operating now. The roster covers entities licensed by CBY-Aden; this evidence base holds no list from the Central Bank of Yemen in Sana'a, so these entries are not a count for all of Yemen. Older counts do not compare with them: the World Bank’s appraisal document for FMIIP (May 2025) reports money-exchanger branches rising from 876 in 2017 to 3,244 in 2019, citing no source, while an International Growth Centre report (February 2026) presents the same pair as World Bank estimates of entities, including exchange firms and microfinance institutions.

On 26 June 2024, a CBY-Aden decision required the exchange companies, exchange establishments and money-transfer agents under its supervision to execute new domestic cash transfers only through the unified money-transfer network. The rule post-dates the survey’s fieldwork, and a rule is not evidence of how transfers actually move.

A hypothesis, not a finding

This Reading’s hypothesis is that money sent between people within Yemen reaches recipients more through exchange companies and other money-transfer providers than into accounts of their own. “Into accounts” means receipt into the recipient’s own account: a transfer can move through the banking system and still be paid out in cash to a recipient without one, so the hypothesis says nothing about the part banks play in moving money. The two routes are not mutually exclusive, and the evidence here does not separate them. The evidence bears on whether recipients held accounts and says nothing about magnitudes: no source here measures what share of households’ cash comes from transfers, how much money moves through each channel, or how often transfers arrive. The bound set out above, by CauseWay’s calculation at least 62.7% of recipients in surveyed areas without an account at a financial institution, itself a survey estimate, bears only on whether recipients could have received the money into such an account of their own; it does not establish the channel, and it neither confirms nor refutes the hypothesis. Separately, the 2014 profile reports that 31.1% of recipients named a money transfer operator and 2.0% a financial institution; it does not show how the others received money, a money transfer operator in the survey is not necessarily an exchange company, and these values do not describe the 2021 wave. This Reading states a hypothesis, not a finding.

Other explanations and limits

  • Other routes. Money may also travel by hand, with travellers or through providers other than exchange companies, and some recipients may be among the 11.9% of adults who had an account; the survey values do not separate these routes.
  • Survey coverage. The survey interviewed 1,000 adults, and its frame excludes Al Baydaa, Al Jawf, Mareb, Sadah, Socotra and several districts elsewhere: areas with about 23% of the population. Money may reach recipients there differently, and the shares say nothing about them; group values rest on smaller samples still.
  • Humanitarian cash. Cash assistance from programmes and agencies is another route into households, and the published values do not show whether any respondent counted it as a remittance. Two Cash Consortium of Yemen studies of aid recipients show how large that route can be where it operates: in three areas surveyed in June 2024, the assistance made up most of the recipients’ cash income, loans from informal networks came second in two of the three areas, and gifts were the smallest share in all three; and in the other study’s sample, in selected villages of Ad-Dali and Ja’ar, some respondents did not count money received by “hawala” (the study’s word) as income. Both studies cover aid recipients only and record no channel for money moving between households, so they neither confirm nor overturn the hypothesis.
  • Currency. Exchange companies change money as well as pay out transfers, so a count of their entries or branches does not show how much of their business is remittances, and a change in the exchange rate changes the rial value of the same transfer.
  • What “remittance” means. In the survey it is money sent or received within Yemen, as adults report it. In CBY-Aden’s balance of payments it is a cross-border flow, in US dollars. In the World Bank’s price data it is a formal product for sending money into Yemen. The three share a word, not a measure.

Price and scale are measured for money from abroad

Two further series concern money sent into Yemen, not within it. The World Bank’s yearly average cost of sending US$200 to Yemen was 2.81% of the amount in 2023; in 2025 Q3, quoted formal products for sending US$200 from Saudi Arabia to Yemen averaged 2.70%, one of the three corridors held here (from the United Arab Emirates the average was 7.53%, lifted by a single high quote, and from the United States 3.92%, computed here from the World Bank's quotes and mixing card, bank-account and cash products). These are prices of sending, not the cost of collecting the money in Yemen or a household’s cost, and they do not cover informal channels. In the balance of payments, CBY-Aden’s annual reports give different values for the same year: the 2024 report put remittances in 2024 at USD 6,245 million, and the 2025 report restated 2024 at USD 3,422.16 million, as the Reading “Same year, different number” explains. Neither value says how many households received money, or through which channel, and the territory these values cover has not been mapped here.

Where the evidence stops

The evidence counts adults, roster entries and prices; it does not observe households’ money. It does not show what share of household cash comes from remittances or how recipients collected the money in the 2021 wave. The two survey shares bound the share of recipients in surveyed areas who lacked an account at a financial institution (at least 62.7%, by CauseWay’s calculation, itself an estimate), but that bound describes the group, not any individual, and does not establish the channel. It does not establish that exchange companies stand in for banks, that more exchange outlets brought more transfers, or that any authority’s rules produced the pattern. A channel value that is missing is unknown, not zero.

How to use the figures

Before relying on these figures, a regulator, donor or provider can check four things:

  • the unit: adults in surveyed areas, not households and not accounts;
  • where the money moved: within Yemen in the survey, from abroad in CBY-Aden’s figures and the World Bank’s price data;
  • the date: survey fieldwork ended in January 2023, and the only weighted channel values are for 2014; for the 2021 wave none usable here is published or held, though World Bank documentation records the item as asked and answered;
  • the status of a provider: a roster entry shows a licence listed for 2026; it does not by itself show that the provider operates now.

What would change this reading?

Four kinds of evidence would test the hypothesis against its alternatives:

  • a household survey module on remittances that records receipt, channel, currency and frequency;
  • weighted channel estimates for domestic remittances: for the 2021 wave none usable here is published or held, though the World Bank documents that the question was asked and answered; and the World Bank has published no later Yemen wave;
  • published figures, from exchange companies, remittance agents or their supervisor, that separate remittance pay-outs from currency exchange, by area;
  • data that separate humanitarian cash from transfers between relatives in what households receive.

If adults who receive transfers received them into accounts or wallets of their own more often than through exchange companies and other money-transfer providers, where the two can be told apart, the hypothesis would fail.

Until then, read the survey shares as the share of adults who sent or received money, not as how much households depend on it.

Related measurement priorities

Each priority below would supply evidence that this Reading says is missing; the link does not mean the priority would settle the Reading.

Measurement priorityP0 · People
A current people-side inclusion baseline
The Global Findex 2025 edition contains 2024 observations for many economies, but Yemen's latest representative account-ownership observation remains 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed, for 2022 (from the Yemen Findex 2021 study fielded in 2022–2023). Major payment-system and reform changes are more recent. The World Bank publishes 2021-wave values for domestic remittances: 17.7% of adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed sent them and 31.9% received them, also by group (shown on /people/); the channels through which the money moved are not shown. Adding a finance module to an existing survey is one route to such a baseline. The Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2022–2023 of the Central Statistical Organization and UNICEF was designed for all 22 governorates (41 enumeration areas could not be visited) and asks one household question on finance, whether any member has a bank account, which its findings report does not tabulate. The World Bank's mobile phone survey of August–September 2022 interviewed 1,297 adults aged 18 and over with mobile phones and records each respondent's area of control, the internationally recognized government or the de facto authorities. For shop credit to households (customers buying from shops on credit) there are local observations, not a baseline: in a 2024 Cash Consortium of Yemen study, 11 of 21 business owners who answered in Ad-Dali and 10 of 21 in Ja’ar said that fewer customers bought on credit when cash assistance was distributed.
Evidence needed: New representative Yemen demand-side survey or equivalent approved microdata with weights and clear coverage, including remittance receipt, channel and frequency.
Decision it would strengthen: A current population measure would allow change since the previous wave to be assessed without projecting reform results onto the population.
Open this measurement priority
Measurement priorityP0 · Providers / Geography
A register of active financial access points
Current official rosters establish selected listing, licensing and event states, but do not provide a complete, geocoded register of active branches, agents, merchants and other service points. The IMF Financial Access Survey, as published in the World Bank's World Development Indicators (series FB.ATM.TOTL.P5, FB.CBK.BRCH.P5 and FB.CBK.DPTR.P3), last reports Yemen for 2015: 5.81 ATMs and 1.5 commercial bank branches per 100,000 adults, and 103.1 depositors with commercial banks per 1,000 adults. The series stops in 2015 and its population denominators are the IMF's; the values are dated historical context, not a current measure of access to, or use of, financial services. Local observations point to a liquidity dimension that registers do not capture: a May 2026 Cash Consortium of Yemen report, in its section on humanitarian multi-purpose cash assistance, records agents lacking enough cash during the Ramadan and Eid holiday period, with waits of four to five hours (from one interview with a programme manager), and funds released only in denominations of YER 100 and 200.
Evidence needed: An authoritative or jointly documented register of individual access points recording type, active status, date, location and services, plus population denominators and road-network data that allow coverage and travel distance or time to be calculated.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would distinguish listing and licensing from operation and observed access before any access or opportunity map is interpreted.

Evidence periodReference years 2021–2024 · CBY-Aden annual reports 2024 and 2025 · IMF Article IV consultation 2025
Same year, different number
Successive annual reports of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden give very different remittance values for 2024. A revision of this size is a measurement event to be explained before it can be read as an economic story.
Evidence periodWorld Bank and G2Px material, May 2024 · reference period of the recipient figure not recorded · Cash Consortium of Yemen study (2026) and report (May 2026) and World Bank project documents (2025–2026) · UNICEF press releases (October and December 2024) · Cash Consortium of Yemen survey of January 2024 (posted online November 2024)
The payment arrived. What happened next?
Material on Yemen’s digital-payment pilot describes transfers paid into fully functional accounts, with recipient choice, for 45,460 recipients. That is an important step in delivery. It is not yet evidence that the accounts stayed part of recipients’ financial lives after the payments.
